readingInstruction: Read 2 Samuel 11:1-12:31. This is the darkest chapter of David’s life. Read it slowly and honestly. Notice how sin grows, how Nathan confronts it, and what God says in response to David’s repentance.
settingTheScene: It is spring, when kings go out to war, but David stays in Jerusalem. From his roof he sees a woman bathing. What follows is adultery, deception, and murder. After months of silence, the prophet Nathan is sent to confront him. The chapters record the cost of David’s sin and the shape of true repentance.
observation: “In the spring of the year, the time when kings go out to battle, David sent Joab… But David remained at Jerusalem” (11:1).
David sees Bathsheba, sends for her, and sleeps with her. She becomes pregnant (11:2-5).
David tries to cover it up by recalling Uriah from battle, and when that fails, has Joab put Uriah in the front line to be killed (11:6-25).
“But the thing that David had done displeased the LORD” (11:27).
Nathan tells a parable about a rich man who takes a poor man’s only lamb, and says, “You are the man!” (12:1-7).
“I anointed you king over Israel… Why have you despised the word of the LORD, to do what is evil in his sight?” (12:7-9).
David says, “I have sinned against the LORD.” Nathan replies, “The LORD has put away your sin; you shall not die” (12:13).
“Nevertheless… the child who is born to you shall die” (12:14). David worships, and later Solomon is born, “and the LORD loved him” (12:15-25).
interpretation:
The sin begins with an idle moment. David was not where he should have been. He sees, wants, takes. He moves from lust to adultery, to the abuse of power, to deception, to murder. At each step he tries to cover the previous sin with a worse one. It is a picture of how sin multiplies. The narrator does not excuse him. The king who should have been guarding justice becomes its violator. The phrase “But David remained at Jerusalem” is where the story starts to unravel.

For a year, he seems to have gotten away with it. But “the thing that David had done displeased the LORD.” God sends Nathan, who tells a story. David’s anger is aroused against the rich man in the parable, and he pronounces judgment. Then Nathan says, “You are the man.” It is the moment of truth. The king who judged others is judged himself.

God’s words through Nathan are heartbreaking. He recounts what he has given David and says, “If this were too little, I would add to you as much more.” David despised God’s word and did evil. It is an act of ingratitude as well as of lust.

David’s response is brief and real. “I have sinned against the LORD.” There is no excuse, no blaming. And Nathan answers with some of the most precious words in the Old Testament: “The LORD has put away your sin; you shall not die.” Forgiveness is immediate and complete. But consequences remain. The child dies, and the sword will not depart from David’s house. Grace does not cancel the effects of sin in this world.

The scene shows both the severity and the mercy of God. He does not ignore sin, even in his favorite. And he does not refuse forgiveness to the one who confesses. At the end, God gives the couple a son, Solomon, whom he loves.
connection: Paul says, “Where sin increased, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5:20). Paul quotes Psalm 32, which David wrote after this episode, in Romans 4:6-8 as a description of justification by faith. Matthew’s genealogy mentions “Uriah’s wife” (Matthew 1:6), reminding us that Jesus came through this broken line. Christ is the greater David who, unlike David, never abused his power, and who laid down his life instead of taking another’s.
application:
Look for places where you are “staying home” when you should be at your post. What is the first step you could take away from temptation?

If you are hiding something, bring it to God now. Do not wait for a Nathan.

Remember that forgiveness is real and complete, even when consequences remain.
prayerPrompts: Confess honestly where you have sinned, and do not cover it.
Ask him to keep you from the “roof” where temptation finds you.
Thank Jesus for bearing the sin you confess.
